answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Azure resource provider: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Top-level resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the account resource representing the Cosmos DB / DocumentDB cluster).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core Azure CLI group az cosmosdb (built-into the az CLI). Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name <account> --resource-group <rg> --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=<region> --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (set kind: 'MongoDB' and capabilities or properties to enable MongoDB API). Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account resource (set kind = 'MongoDB' and consistency/offer_type/etc.).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: MongoDB connection strings follow mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://. For Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB MongoDB API) the host suffix is typically <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com. Non-SRV form uses port 10255. Typical options required: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false. Example non-SRV: mongodb://<username>@<account>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Example SRV: mongodb+srv://<username>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Cosmos DB throughput: Request Units (RU/s) for provisioned throughput (can be fixed or autoscale). There is also a serverless mode for supported API/accounts. It is not billed by vCores for the MongoDB API (use RUs or serverless).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary supported auth for MongoDB API is account keys / username+password (username typically in the form <username>@<account> and password is the primary key). Resource tokens (for SDKs) exist for Cosmos DB SQL API, but MongoDB API commonly uses account keys. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) data-plane authentication is not generally available for the MongoDB wire protocol (so drivers do not authenticate to the MongoDB API with AAD tokens in typical setups).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., the Node.js mongodb driver or Mongoose). Do not use the Cosmos DB SQL-specific SDK if you intend to speak MongoDB protocol; there is no separate MongoDB-specific Azure SDK — the MongoDB driver is the correct client.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Historically Cosmos DB / DocumentDB did not expose built-in vector index types via the MongoDB API. If vector search is required you normally integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or an external vector engine. Therefore there is no service-native MongoDB command to create DiskANN/HNSW/IVF indexes in the MongoDB API (no native db.collection.createIndex([...], {type:'hnsw' ...}) support).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text search is typically done by integrating Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search (indexing Cosmos DB containers into an Azure Search index). Hybrid search (semantic + vector) is done in Azure Cognitive Search or an external search service; Cosmos DB's MongoDB API itself does not provide a first-class full-text + vector search engine.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API implements a subset of the MongoDB wire protocol. Supported server versions historically lag upstream (common supported compatibility levels were 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 4.4 and later additions), and not all MongoDB features are available. Commonly missing or limited features include some admin commands, server-side JavaScript, certain aggregation stages or collation behaviors, and some transactional or index features depending on the compatibility version. Expect to verify support for advanced features (change streams, transactions, some geo/aggregation operators) against the account's compatibility version.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for the SQL API but it historically does not fully emulate the MongoDB wire protocol. For MongoDB API development you should run a local MongoDB server (official Docker image mongo) on the default port 27017, using the same MongoDB server version that your Cosmos account claims to support. There is no fully-featured local emulator that gives the exact Cosmos MongoDB behavior.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB exposes a Change Feed for the core (SQL) API; support for MongoDB change streams has been historically limited or unavailable. If you need change notifications on the MongoDB API, you typically must either use Cosmos DB Change Feed (via the SQL API) or poll/implement application-level hooks; there is no simple enablement flag for MongoDB change streams in older versions.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Data-plane tooling is provided via the Azure management/control plane (Azure Resource Manager) and the az cosmosdb CLI. There isn't a separate special-purpose MCP agent required for Cosmos DB; the general Azure management plane and az CLI cover provisioning and management. For data-plane operations use the MongoDB drivers against the account endpoints.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: The original preview service was called Azure DocumentDB; that product evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. "DocumentDB" historically refers to the SQL/JSON API implementation inside Cosmos DB. The Cosmos DB MongoDB API is a protocol compatibility layer (not the open-source MongoDB or Apache 'DocumentDB' project). The old name 'DocumentDB' is essentially superseded by Cosmos DB.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the MongoDB API the underlying engine is Azure Cosmos DB's proprietary storage and execution engine with a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol layer. That means application code using standard MongoDB drivers will mostly work, but there are behavioral differences (query semantics, indexing, RU-based throttling, and some unsupported operators/commands). Test to confirm behavior for advanced features and tune RU usage.

answers.question: Which database name will the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_customer_360_01 for all sample objects (collections, indexes, test data).

answers.question: Which environment variable contains the connection string for the cluster?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime; do not hard-code or write the secret into files.

answers.question: What exact Mongoose connection invocation and options should the sample use to connect to the DocumentDB Mongo endpoint?
answers.answer: Example Node.js/Mongoose connect call: await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: false, replicaSet: 'globaldb', retryWrites: false }); Replace placeholders in DOCUMENTDB_URI as necessary. Use TLS/SSL and disable retryWrites as recommended for Cosmos MongoDB API.

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for efficient upserts and lookups?
answers.answer: Create a unique index on the stable customer ID used for identity resolution. Example Mongo shell command: db.customers.createIndex({ customerId: 1 }, { unique: true, background: true });

answers.question: If change streams are not available, how will the sample perform idempotent upserts without losing other source sub-documents?
answers.answer: Use MongoDB upsert semantics with findOneAndUpdate and $set on nested sub-documents for each source. Example: db.customers.findOneAndUpdate({ customerId: id }, { $set: { 'sources.crm': crmAttrs, 'sources.ecom': ecomAttrs, updatedAt: new Date() } }, { upsert: true, returnDocument: 'after' }); This merges fields under sources.* and avoids overwriting unrelated source sub-documents.
